newsitem.title: USA: Minority groups call on Clinton to fix welfare law.
newsitem.headline: Minority groups call on Clinton to fix welfare law.

text.p: Minority activists on Thursday warned President Bill Clinton not to back away from his promise to "fix" a landmark welfare law that makes deep cuts in federal aid to legal immigrants.

Telling the White House not to take their political support for granted, Hispanic, Jewish and Asian-American officials also said they were watching closely to see whether Clinton appointed minorities to fill vacancies in his Cabinet.

The welfare law, signed by Clinton in August, cuts federal spending by $54 billion over six years. About $24 billion in reductions come from denying Food Stamps, disability and other federal aid to legal immigrants.
In announcing his decision to sign the bill, Clinton criticised the immigrant provisions and promised he would push Congress to restore some of the cuts next year.

White House officials held private meetings this week to decide how much money to include for welfare in the president's 1998 budget plan. The news conference was designed to keep the heat on Clinton as those decisions are made.

"Communities are bracing for an extraordinary humanitairan crisis this spring, when elderly and disabled immigrants ... (are) cut off critical safety net programmes," said Cecilia Munoz, deputy vice president of National Council of La Raza.
Pointing out Latino and Asian voters turned out in big numbers in November, Munoz said much of their support was based on Clinton's promise to restore some cuts in the law.
"We expect the president to keep faith ... we expect him to stand firm," Munoz said.

California Democratic Representative Xavier Becerra said Clinton's decisions on Cabinet vacancies and welfare would send an important message whether minorities "can depend on the president and his administration ... to keep his promise."

Becerra said the Hispanic Caucus had asked to meet with Clinton, adding he was concerned about reports the White House might ask Congress to delay cuts in aid to legal immigrants rather than fighting to restore them.
Aside from cuts in aid to immigrants, Clinton has also said he wants to include money to mitigate some of the $28 billion in Food Stamp cuts in the welfare law.
